topic: Fairness in Topology: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem and the Stolen Necklace Problem
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Mathematics or Computer Science

sections.title: The Hook: The Disputed Treasure
sections.content: Introduce a scenario where two thieves, Alice and Bob, have stolen a necklace made of different types of precious beads (e.g., rubies and emeralds). They want to split the necklace so that each person receives exactly half of each type of bead. The challenge is to find the minimum number of cuts required to achieve this 'fair split'.
sections.example: Visualize a long string with 10 red beads and 8 green beads arranged randomly. How can we cut it so Alice and Bob both get 5 red and 4 green?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Intermediate Value Theorem (1D Case)
sections.content: Before tackling the necklace, introduce the 1D version of the logic. If a continuous function changes from a negative value to a positive value, it must pass through zero. This ensures that on a continuous 'sliding scale' of a cut, there is always a point of perfect 50/50 balance for one type of bead.
sections.example: An animation of a knife sliding along a string of only red beads. At the start, Alice has 0%; at the end, she has 100%. Therefore, there must be a spot in the middle where she has exactly 50%.

sections.title: The Core Concept: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
sections.content: Define the theorem formally but visually: For any continuous map from an n-sphere (Sn) to Euclidean n-space (Rn), there exists at least one pair of antipodal points (points exactly opposite each other on the sphere) that map to the same value.
sections.example: The 'Earth Example': At any given moment, there are two points exactly opposite each other on Earth's surface that have the exact same temperature and the exact same barometric pressure.

sections.title: Mapping the Necklace to a Sphere
sections.content: Explain how a necklace with 'k' types of beads can be represented as a mathematical space. We represent the possible cutting positions as coordinates on a high-dimensional sphere. A point on this sphere represents a specific way to partition the necklace between Alice and Bob.
sections.example: A 3D animation showing a circular necklace being projected onto a sphere, where moving to the 'opposite' side of the sphere represents giving Bob everything Alice previously had, and vice-versa.

sections.title: The Elegant Solution
sections.content: Apply Borsuk-Ulam to the necklace. If there are 'k' types of beads, we map the sphere to R^k (where each dimension is the amount of one bead type Alice receives). The theorem guarantees a pair of antipodal points with the same value. Since antipodal points represent a total swap of shares, the only way they can be 'equal' is if both shares are exactly 50/50.
sections.example: Show a necklace with 2 types of beads. By the theorem, only 2 cuts are needed. The animation shows the cuts shifting until the 'balance' function for both bead types hits the zero-difference point simultaneously.

sections.title: Conclusion and Real-World Intuition
sections.content: Summarize that for 'k' types of beads, 'k' cuts are always sufficient. Highlight how topology—a study of shapes—provides a definitive answer to a problem of discrete fairness and resource allocation.
sections.example: Final shot of Alice and Bob walking away happy with their perfectly equal shares, overlaid with a geometric grid showing the 'path to fairness' on a sphere.
